abstract: The brain uses regularities in the sensory environment to anticipate upcoming events, but whether predictions about stimulus identity and timing rely on dissociable neural mechanisms remains unclear. Here, we independently manipulated the temporal structure of acoustic sequences (rhythmic vs. jittered) and stimulus deviance of sequence elements (deviants vs. standards) while recording local field potentials (LFPs) and multiunit activity (AMUA) simultaneously from ventral and dorsal medial geniculate body (MGB) and cortical layers in 9 female anesthetized rats. Temporal structure robustly modulated neural responses throughout the auditory thalamocortical system. LFP responses were stronger for jittered than rhythmic stimulation across all layers of both primary and non-primary auditory cortex, with effects spanning early and later poststimulus intervals. AMUA responses showed a complementary temporal-predictability effect in both dorsal and ventral MGB, with stronger responses to jittered than rhythmic stimuli. In contrast, stimulus deviance effects were strongly dependent on temporal context and recording site. Deviant standard differences were enhanced under jittered stimulation in cortex and in early MGB responses, whereas later MGB responses showed a context dependent reversal. Finally, AMUA based Granger analyses revealed sustained jitter specific directed influences from both dorsal and ventral MGB toward multiple cortical layers during the poststimulus period. Together, these findings demonstrate that temporal regularity robustly modulates auditory thalamocortical responses and is associated with changes in directed interactions between thalamus and cortex. Responses to stimulus deviance, in turn, depend on temporal context and recording site. These findings reveal distinct but interacting neural signatures of temporal regularity and stimulus deviance in the auditory thalamocortical system.
